lead: Today the Syriac calendar remembers the Holy Mother of God for the ears of grain, asking her prayers over the ripening harvest, and also St Pachomius, father of monks who live in community. The readings fit the day beautifully. Paul speaks of sowing and reaping, of a God “who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food”. In Luke a woman blesses the mother of Jesus, and Jesus answers that those who hear the word of God and obey it are blessed. Mary is blessed in both ways. The key words are sowing and hearing.

set: Chapters 8 and 9 of 2 Corinthians are about the collection Paul was gathering among his Gentile churches for the poor Christians of Jerusalem (see also Romans 15:25–27; 1 Corinthians 16:1–4). For Paul this gift was more than charity. It was a sign of the unity between the Gentile churches and the mother church from which the Gospel had come to them. Many scholars think chapters 8 and 9 may once have been separate notes, but they belong together in theme.
str: v. 6: the rule of the harvest: sparingly or bountifully.
vv. 8–10: God's power to provide, with Psalm 112 and an echo of Isaiah 55.
kw: From this word comes the English “hilarious”. Paul's phrase recalls the Greek Old Testament of Proverbs 22:8, which has a line not in the Hebrew: “God blesses a cheerful and generous man.” The point is not noise but gladness: giving that comes from joy, not pressure.
Literally “with blessings”. The same word, eulogia, is used in 9:5 for the gift itself. A gift given generously is a blessing for the one who gives and the one who receives.
vv: the one who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and the one who sows bountifully will also reap bountifully.
A farmer who keeps back his seed out of fear will have a poor harvest. Generosity is a kind of trust in God.
for God loves a cheerful giver.
God looks at the heart of the giver more than at the size of the gift, as Jesus saw in the widow's two coins (Mark 12:41–44).
He who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food will supply and multiply your seed for sowing
These words echo Isaiah 55:10, where the rain gives “seed to the sower and bread to the eater”, a picture of God's word that does not return empty.
ch: The Church reads this passage when she speaks of almsgiving and the sharing of goods. The Catechism teaches that giving alms to the poor is a witness to fraternal charity and a work of justice pleasing to God (CCC 2462), and it lists the corporal works of mercy (CCC 2447). On a day when the Church prays over the harvest, Paul reminds us that every harvest is God's gift, given to be shared.

r.h: Blessed are those who hear the word of God
set: Jesus has just answered those who said he cast out demons by Beelzebul (11:14–26). A woman in the crowd, moved by his words, cries out a blessing on his mother. This short scene is found only in Luke. It recalls Elizabeth's blessing in 1:42–45 and Mary's own words, “all generations will call me blessed” (1:48).
str: v. 27: a woman blesses the mother of Jesus.
v. 28: Jesus' answer: blessed are those who hear and keep the word of God.
kw: The word of the Beatitudes (6:20–22). It speaks of the happiness that comes from God, not of good luck.

A small Greek word with a large meaning. It can mean “no, rather” or “yes, but even more”. Here Jesus does not deny the woman's praise; he widens it and goes deeper: what makes a person truly blessed is hearing and keeping the word.
The verb means to guard or keep watch over something precious. Luke twice says that Mary “treasured” all these things in her heart (2:19, 51).
vv: Blessed is the womb that bore you and the breasts that nursed you!
A common way in that world of praising a son by praising his mother. Without knowing it, the woman fulfils Mary's prophecy that all generations would call her blessed.
Blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and obey it!

Jesus does not set Mary aside. He names the deeper reason for her blessedness. She is the first to hear the word and keep it: “Here am I, the servant of the Lord; let it be with me according to your word” (1:38).
ch: The Second Vatican Council cites this passage when it speaks of Mary during her Son's public ministry: he declared blessed those who hear and keep the word of God, as she was faithfully doing (Lumen Gentium 58). St Augustine taught that Mary was more blessed in receiving the faith of Christ than in conceiving the flesh of Christ (On Holy Virginity 3, in substance). Mary's motherhood and her faith are not rivals. She conceived the Word in her heart before she conceived him in her womb.

qa: Is Jesus correcting the woman, or lowering his mother?

No. The word he uses can mean “yes, but even more”. Elsewhere Luke shows Mary as the model of one who hears the word and keeps it (1:38, 45; 2:19, 51; 8:21). Jesus' answer is the highest praise of his mother, and it opens her blessedness to every disciple who listens as she did.
rite: The Syriac tradition keeps three commemorations of the Mother of God tied to the farming year: for the seeds in January, for the ears of grain in May, and for the vines in August. In Kerala, where life still follows the rains and the harvest, these days teach that Mary prays for our daily bread as well as for our souls. Today is also the memory of Mar Pachomios (Pachomius), the Egyptian monk of the fourth century who first gathered monks into a common life under a written rule. Our monks and religious owe much to him.
study: Am I a sparing sower or a bountiful one, with my time, my money and my kindness?
How can I, like Mary, hear the word of God this week and keep it in my heart?
